items.t: Newsom commutes all 548 California death sentences in final months as governor
items.s: California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on the state’s death row to life without the possibility of parole, according to his letter and several news outlets. The move means none of them can be executed under future administrations.
p: Newsom announced the decision on Thursday in a letter, saying he was using his constitutional clemency power. The Democrat, who is term limited and is leaving office after eight years, is widely discussed as a possible presidential candidate in 2028.

The Guardian reported that the decision affects 529 men and 19 women. Newsom’s office said 220 of those sentenced have waited 15 years or more for habeas counsel, the lawyers they are entitled to in order to challenge their cases, and 139 have waited 20 years or more. Without the moratorium he imposed in 2019, the office said, 45 people had exhausted their appeals and could have been executed immediately.

In his letter, Newsom wrote that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values. The BBC quoted him saying the state “cannot morally kill them”, and that he believed the state’s death penalty system “is a failure”. He also said he alone bears responsibility for the decision.

California has not carried out an execution since 2006, and the BBC noted that only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978. The Guardian reported that Newsom dismantled the death row chamber at San Quentin prison and moved condemned people to facilities with more freedom of movement.

The announcement came weeks after the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, which the Guardian said had sparked outrage and renewed calls for a nationwide pause on capital punishment. The BBC described it as a botched execution in late September.

Newsom said the California Supreme Court must review and approve clemency for people convicted of multiple felonies. DW, citing the Los Angeles Times, reported that Newsom could commute about 40 percent of the sentences directly, while the court would have to approve 382 others, roughly 70 percent, according to his office.

The American Civil Liberties Union praised the move, as did Bryan Stevenson and Martin Luther King III. Jess Nichol, sister of Polly Klaas, who was killed in 1993, said in a statement that execution had no bearing on her recovery. Governors of both parties have taken similar steps before, including an Illinois Republican who commuted 167 death sentences in 2003.

The federal picture differs. President Donald Trump has described capital punishment as an essential tool, and he reinstated the federal death penalty by executive order in 2025. The BBC reported that no federal executions have been carried out since then.
items.cav: The sources give different figures for how many commutations need court approval: DW and the Los Angeles Times cite 382, while DW’s own 40 percent claim does not add up with that number. The BBC reports that all 548 sentences were converted, while others note the court review requirement, so the final legal status of each case is not clear from these reports.
items.op: Clemency at the end of a term can be legitimate, but it should not depend on one official’s timing or unclear legal process. Californians deserve a complete public account of which commutations are final and which await judicial approval. A justice system that changes with the calendar of a governor’s office is fragile, and the state should set this policy in law.

items.t: Europe's hoax airline bomb threats remain unexplained as Russia suspicions grow
items.s: A wave of bomb threats against European airlines and airports has so far produced no hard evidence of who sent them, according to the BBC. Suspicion has nonetheless fallen on Russia because of other hostile incidents across the continent.
p: The threats arrived in quick succession, each aimed at a different airline or airport. In nearly all cases they were treated as credible enough to divert the aircraft concerned. In Italy, fighter jets were scrambled to escort one flight. London’s Heathrow was a notable exception. Every threat later proved false, though the BBC notes that this does not mean future warnings will be hoaxes.

The simultaneous and co-ordinated pattern has led some people to point to Russia. The BBC describes a run of recent incidents: cyber-attacks and mysterious drone sightings over sensitive sites earlier this year, the remote hacking of supermarket freezers and a blood bank, and a suspicious incident on Poland’s border with Russia. In August, a drone attack on Leipzig Halle airport in Germany was publicly blamed on Moscow by the German interior minister.

Some commentators argue, on circumstantial grounds, that the airline threats fit what is often called hybrid or grey-zone warfare. Such actions damage infrastructure or society while staying anonymous and deniable, and they tend to fall short of the threshold that would trigger Nato’s Article 5 collective defence clause.

The BBC reports that Moscow is angry at Nato’s support for Ukraine. Russian bloggers have also argued that if Ukrainian drones are making Russian airports unsafe, and Western sanctions keep Russian airlines out of European airspace, Western countries should feel similar pain.

Still, as of Thursday evening, no hard evidence had emerged linking the hoaxes to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups they control. One email, sent on Thursday morning to airport authorities in Rome and signed “Fighters of the Male State”, may refer to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion, an ultra-right group banned by a Moscow court in 2021. The BBC notes that the group kept tens of thousands of followers on Telegram. It also warns that the name could be used by another group, and that even a genuine email is unlikely to give police the leads they need.

The BBC argues that national police, airport authorities and transport ministries should not start from their assumptions about the likeliest culprits. Instead, they should follow concrete leads, if they can find them.
items.cav: This is a single-outlet analysis, and the BBC itself says there is no hard evidence linking the hoaxes to Russia, Iran or proxies. The link between the Rome email and the Muzhskoi Legion is described as likely, not confirmed, and the email could come from another group.
items.op: Without proof, blaming a hostile state is a shortcut that can damage public trust and distort the investigation. Authorities owe passengers a transparent account of who is responsible and what evidence supports it. Speculation should not replace detective work.

items.t: Met police urge more victims to come forward as Russell Brand faces two further rape allegations
items.s: The lead detective in the case against Russell Brand has urged other possible victims to come forward, after it emerged the comedian is under investigation for two further rape allegations. Police say files have gone to the Crown Prosecution Service.
p: Brand, 51, was convicted at Southwark crown court of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three women over five years, during the peak of his career, according to the Guardian. Jurors cleared him of two other rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault after a four-week trial.

Det Supt Andy Furphy, who leads the Metropolitan police’s work on the case, called Brand a predator whose conduct grew more serious as his profile rose. Speaking after the verdict, he said he believed further victims might exist and that the inquiry was still active.

The force confirmed that Brand had been questioned under caution over two more rape allegations, each made by a different woman. A spokesperson said the files had been passed to prosecutors and that detectives were in regular contact with them. The inquiry, Operation Actinolite, drew on more than 100 witnesses, over 1,400 documents and more than 340 statements.

Pre-trial legal papers, as reported by the Guardian, pointed to outstanding charges linked to a woman who spoke about Brand in a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary. She alleged he groomed her while she was a 16-year-old schoolgirl. Furphy would not discuss open lines of inquiry, but urged anyone affected by Brand to contact officers, promising specialist support.

Brand also faces civil proceedings in London and the United States. One woman, who began a claim at the High Court in London, says he assaulted her at his Los Angeles home in 2008, removing her clothing and trying to force oral sex. Brand denies the allegations, which his lawyers have called “fundamentally dishonest”. The claim, lodged last year and paused until the criminal trial ended, reportedly seeks damages of up to £100,000.

Furphy described the verdict as a possible turning point that could encourage others to report sexual crimes, and linked the period to a wider lad culture. He also said Brand had come close to the limits of acceptable conduct during the trial through his podcasts and media appearances, without crossing them.
None of the new allegations or civil claims has been tested in court. The police have not said when, or whether, charging decisions will follow.
items.cav: The reports of further allegations and outstanding charges come from police statements and pre-trial documents as relayed by the Guardian, and the report of other women making allegations is second-hand. The civil claim details come from court papers, and Brand’s denial is given through his lawyers.
items.op: Public confidence depends on keeping convictions, open investigations and unproven civil claims clearly separate. The police appeal for witnesses is right, but every complainant and the accused deserve a fair process. Fame should never shield anyone from scrutiny, and it should never replace evidence in court.

items.t: Cancer diagnoses in England reach record high, but NHS still misses key waiting-time targets
items.s: More than 373,000 people were diagnosed with cancer in England in 2024, the highest annual figure on record. Experts say the health service is still missing its targets for diagnosis and treatment speed.
p: England recorded its highest cancer diagnosis total yet in 2024, with the latest registration statistics putting the figure above 373,000 people. Averaged out, that works out to more than 1,000 new diagnoses each day, as reported by The Guardian.
The daily average rose to 1,021 in 2024, compared with 972 the year before. Prostate, breast, lung and bowel cancers made up roughly half of all new cases.
There was also some progress on how advanced cancers were when detected. Around 56.7% of first-time cancers were caught at stage 1 or 2 in 2024, up from 55.8% in 2023.

Prof Peter Johnson, the NHS national clinical director for cancer, described the trend as heading in the right direction and credited frontline staff. He said testing is increasingly being brought nearer to patients who need it.

Specialists urged restraint. Monthly NHS data for August showed 78.6% of urgent suspected-cancer referrals were diagnosed or cleared within 28 days, short of the 80% goal. Only 71.9% of patients began treatment within 62 days of an urgent referral or consultant upgrade, far below the 85% target.

Dr Ian Walker of Cancer Research UK argued that too many people are still diagnosed late and that the NHS needs more help to reverse this. He urged the government to follow through on its national cancer plan for England, which committed to better early diagnosis, faster waiting times and wider access to treatment.

Dr Hilary Williams of the Royal College of Physicians pointed to an ageing population and obesity as contributors to the rise, with obesity described as a significant risk factor that is often underestimated. Steven McIntosh of Macmillan Cancer Support warned that the national picture hides ongoing inequalities linked to where people live and who they are. Rachael Franklin of Breast Cancer Now encouraged women to attend screening when invited.
items.cav: The diagnosis totals are an annual count for 2024, while the waiting-time figures cover only August. The report does not say how much of the increase reflects population growth versus better detection, and the commentators quoted are clinicians and charity representatives rather than independent analysts.
items.op: A record number of diagnoses is not, on its own, a success. If the NHS is finding more cancers while missing its own 28-day and 62-day targets, patients are bearing the cost of that gap. The government should publish a dated plan with named accountability for closing it.

items.t: Paraguayan president resigns as Ueno Bank collapse leaves millions without access to their savings
items.s: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña resigned on Thursday as a banking crisis deepened, just as lawmakers moved to impeach him. The collapse of Ueno Bank has cut off access to accounts for nearly three million customers.
p: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña resigned on Thursday amid a banking crisis, according to Euronews, just as the Chamber of Deputies was voting to impeach him. He announced his decision in a video posted to X while lawmakers were debating his impeachment. He said he was stepping down in the interest of the stability of the country and social peace.

The crisis centres on Ueno Bank, which the central bank took control of on Tuesday, citing a severe capital shortfall. The lender had close to three million customers, who suddenly found their accounts out of reach. Its app, cards and transfers stopped working, and branches locked their doors, leaving depositors queuing outside with no way to withdraw their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open accounts at other banks crashed their mobile apps, adding to public panic.

Regulators investigating the bank reported poorly documented lending and expenses that had been wrongly recorded as assets. Once the books were corrected, Ueno’s capital fell below the legal minimum, which led to the seizure. Euronews said the size of the shortfall was described in the reporting only in general terms.

In a video, Peña apologised to the public and said he had never intended to betray their trust. He expressed contrition but stopped short of accepting responsibility for the crisis, which has plunged a country long valued by foreign investors for its stability into financial and political turmoil. He had held a stake in a company related to Ueno Bank until last year.

Ueno grew from an obscure finance company into a household name in less than five years. After receiving its banking license in 2023, it offered cash-back deals on groceries, expanded to more than 70 locations and sponsored the national football team. It claimed more than 60% of Paraguay’s adults as customers. Peña also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the bank’s predecessor, to run the central bank, which supervises the lender.

Public money was heavily concentrated at the bank. As of last month, Ueno reported about $800 million (€712 million) in public deposits, roughly a quarter of its total, including funds from the state pension and health fund. ABC Color reported that central bank inspectors had found a pattern of risky lending to insiders in June. Euronews also reported that nearly $39 million (€35 million) went to three companies tied to the owners on a single day in September 2025. Peña dismissed such concerns as a smear campaign as recently as last month.

Anger has spilled onto the streets. Long lines formed at Ueno branches in the capital, Asunción, on Tuesday and Wednesday, and protesters marched to Congress. One protester, Luis Pineda, accused Peña and the Colorado Party of stealing all savings. Ruling party deputy Alejandro Aquilera said more than three million Paraguayans had been harmed. Vice President Pedro Alliana is set to take office, according to the summary of the report.
items.cav: The sources differ on the sequence of events: the article says the resignation came as the impeachment vote was under way, while the summary says Peña was impeached after resigning. Alliana’s succession appears only in the summary, and the size of Ueno’s capital shortfall is not quantified. The inspection findings and the insider-lending figures are second-hand, relying on ABC Color and the reporting of Euronews.
items.op: Paraguayans were promised stability, and the state’s own pensions and health funds were left exposed. Transparency at the central bank and clear accountability for the president’s ties to Ueno are now essential. Warnings were ignored for months, and no official should be allowed to dismiss scrutiny as a smear.

items.t: US tech stocks slide as investors bet on tougher rules after midterm results
items.s: The Nasdaq was on track for its worst day in 18 months on Thursday, as investors priced in possible tighter rules for the technology sector’s datacentre expansion after the US midterm elections.
p: The Nasdaq composite slumped by as much as 5% in volatile trading on Wall Street, according to The Guardian, and tumbled into what the paper described as “correction territory”, more than 10% below its recent record high. The tech-heavy index was heading for its biggest one-day fall since the tariffs Donald Trump announced in April 2025.

The sell-off was led by chip stocks. The memory maker SanDisk fell 19% and the hard drive maker Western Digital dropped 16.5%. Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the tech boom, was the biggest faller on the Dow Jones industrial average, down 6.7%, followed by Goldman Sachs at 5.7%.

Analysts pointed to expectations that Democratic governors will restrict the rollout of new datacentres after the party won a series of gubernatorial races this week. Voters in several local ballots across the country had also rejected datacentre projects, the report said. Worries over heavy spending on datacentres spread to other stock markets worldwide.

The Dow was down more than 1,500 points, or 2.8%, in early afternoon trading, at 51,868 points, while the S&P 500 fell 3.7%. The VIX, Wall Street’s so-called fear index, jumped 40% to its highest level since the early weeks of the Iran war. Britain’s FTSE 100 closed 0.4% lower at 10782.66 after an early rally faded.

The fall reversed a strong rally on Wednesday, when US stocks posted their biggest daily gain in months on hopes that the Democrats’ midterm success could restrain the White House. Trump had celebrated record highs on Truth Social, writing that the stock market had just hit another record and that retirement accounts were “through the roof”.

Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, described a “complete capitulation-level event” in tech stocks. He said the market was selling everything and that it needed to find some stability first. Tech analyst Dan Ives warned that Democrats taking control, especially of the Senate, would create significant hurdles for technology legislation over the next two years, and that the pace of datacentre buildout would slow.

Ted Parkhill, founder and CEO of Incline Investment Management, said the market was moving from promise to price in the tech boom. He added that not every stock tied to the boom was priced appropriately at present, and that there would be a lot of turmoil ahead.
items.cav: The figures are intraday readings from early afternoon trading, so the final closing moves may differ. The expected crackdown on datacentres is based on analysts’ expectations and voter results; the sources do not describe any specific new rule or which governors would act. Ives’s warning about the Senate is his own forecast.
items.op: Markets are pricing in a policy shift that has not yet been written into law, and that is the real problem. Investors reacting to expected scrutiny of datacentres deserve clear rules, a transparent process and a timetable, not rumours of a crackdown. Predictable regulation serves both the industry and the voters who have already said no.

items.t: Russell Brand convicted of rape and sexual assault by London jury, to be sentenced Monday
items.s: Comedian and actor Russell Brand has been found guilty by a London jury of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He denies the charges, was remanded in custody, and is due to be sentenced on Monday.
p: A jury at Southwark Crown Court in London returned its verdicts on Thursday after a four-week trial. Brand, 51, was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was cleared of two other rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault, according to the BBC and Al Jazeera.

The offences were said to span 1999 to 2009, the years in which Brand rose from stand-up work in small venues to television and Hollywood success. Prosecutors described him as a ruthless and manipulative sexual predator who used his fame to pressure women. Reports differ on the detail: the BBC says six women gave evidence, while Euronews describes four women and offences between 2005 and 2009.

The jury of eight men and four women deliberated for more than eight hours over two days, according to AFP. Brand closed his eyes and showed little emotion as the verdicts were read, the reports say. He has denied all the charges, saying the encounters were consensual or that the allegations were reinvented after a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and reporting in The Sunday Times.

Judge Joel Bennathan told Brand to expect a “significant custodial term”. He refused bail, citing Brand’s “considerable resources” and the risk that he might not return for sentencing. The judge said he regretted the hardship to Brand’s children, whom Brand had wanted to see over the weekend.

The Metropolitan Police said its investigation into further complaints “remains ongoing”. The BBC and The Guardian report that Brand is under investigation for two further rape allegations, and The Guardian says police have sent files to the Crown Prosecution Service. These claims have not been tested in court, and no further charges have been reported.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy praised the women who came forward, saying their bravery made the outcome possible. Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, had argued that the alleged victims waited years to go to police and that the media coverage made a fair trial impossible. Outside court, Winter also made a remark to Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin that drew attention, according to The Guardian.
The maximum penalty for rape in the UK is life imprisonment, Euronews reports. Brand’s sentence will be decided by the judge on Monday, and the convictions remain subject to any appeal.
items.cav: Sources disagree on the number of women, the time span and some counts, so the figures here are attributed to specific outlets. The further allegations are reported as under investigation, not as charges, and the Euronews reference to a 16-year-old complainant is second-hand.
items.op: A conviction shows that fame offers no shield from the criminal law, and that principle matters more than the celebrity. Sentencing should now rest only on what the jury found. Any further allegations must go through the same open, evidence-based process before anyone is judged on them.

items.t: Hoax bomb threats disrupt dozens of European flights as officials weigh possible links
items.s: Hoax bomb threats forced planes into emergency landings and diversions across Europe on Thursday, and officials are still examining whether the incidents were coordinated. No device was found on any affected aircraft.
p: Threats on Thursday disrupted at least 25 flights, according to one report, and some aircraft were forced into emergency landings. Routes touched Italy, Ireland, the UK, Spain, Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Finland, Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Portugal, France, Greece, Serbia and Czechia. Airlines involved included Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Wizz Air, Finnair, easyJet and LOT Polish Airlines. Every plane landed safely, and searches turned up nothing suspicious.

A separate count from DW put the number at a minimum of a dozen commercial flights that landed unscheduled or under high alert, citing national authorities. The two tallies do not match, and neither offers a single consistent figure.

In Britain, Heathrow and Birmingham airports received overnight warnings, which specialist police investigators judged to be hoaxes. The Metropolitan Police said four aircraft linked to Heathrow had been targeted, and a police spokesperson said that after an assessment no security issues had been identified.

The day followed a similar wave on Tuesday, when seven planes were searched or diverted, and a flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted on Monday. Counting all of these, one account puts the total for the week at no fewer than 33 affected flights.

Investigators said they still had no evidence that a hostile terror group or a state such as Russia or Iran was orchestrating the hoaxes, though inquiries across Europe continue. The EU transport commissioner, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, said it was too early to say whether the incidents were connected, while stressing that threats against civilians were unacceptable.

Emails sent to airports in Rome and Sofia were reportedly signed “fighters of the Male State”, according to sources at Aeroporti di Roma and a text seen by Agence France-Presse. The movement is described as a Russian far-right group whose founder did not comment on or claim the threats. A Kremlin spokesperson dismissed blaming Moscow as absurd.

Italy’s defence minister, Guido Crosetto, argued that the hoaxes amount to what he called under-threshold warfare, deliberately kept below the level at which blame can be assigned. In France, media reports said the pilot of an Aer Lingus flight diverted to Évreux was being questioned after initially refusing to land at a military base.

The episode came days after cyber-attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems. Aviation experts quoted by one outlet said that while fake threats are common, the volume of apparently credible ones points to coordination.
items.cav: The sources disagree on the scale, with 25 flights in one account and at least a dozen in the other. The “Male State” attribution comes from unnamed sources and a text seen by AFP, not from a claim of responsibility, and any link to the fridge attacks is unproven.
items.op: Whoever is sending these hoaxes is betting that uncertainty will do the work for them, and so far it is. Governments should publish what they know about the threats and the evidence for any attribution. Travellers and airlines deserve clear findings, not fog.

items.t: Russell Brand in court: the man in the dock was not the showman viewers knew
items.s: A BBC reporter who covered Russell Brand's rape trial at Southwark Crown Court says the man in the dock looked nothing like the flamboyant comedian of his peak fame years. The jury found him guilty of one rape and three sexual assault charges and cleared him of other counts.
p: The BBC’s reporter, who sat a short distance behind Brand in the press seats, describes a defendant who seemed far removed from the television and comedy persona that many people remember from his peak fame years. Over the course of the trial, Brand sat mostly still in a glass-walled dock, showing little visible emotion as the allegations against him were set out in detail over several days.

After a three-week trial, the 51-year-old was found guilty of one charge of rape and three charges of sexual assault. The jury found him not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault. According to the report, the allegations covered a period from 1999 to 2009 and were brought by six women.

The reporter contrasts the courtroom manner with the evidence. Brand was polite and respectful, holding doors open and thanking court staff. The complainants, by contrast, described a brash and sexually demanding man who, they said, did not accept no for an answer. Some of his old public style did surface outside the building, where he made a beeline for reporters and, on the first day, said he felt “blessed”.

The coverage also recorded several odd moments. On the first day a man who resembled Brand arrived by car and drew shouted questions before the real Brand stepped out. That man appeared on most days of the trial, and the reporter says it was never clear who he was. Brand, who now presents himself as a Christian influencer, wore several crucifixes, and was seen once handling what looked like prayer beads.

The reporter says the testimony was harrowing and graphic. Women who gave evidence did so behind a screen, and the reporter found their accounts deeply moving. Brand’s composure rarely cracked. At times he closed his eyes for several seconds, which the reporter suggests may have been prayer or meditation, though this is only an impression. One complainant told the court that blood and faeces had been left on Brand’s bed sheets after she was raped at his house.
items.cav: This is one reporter’s first-hand impression of courtroom demeanour, not an official account, and the report does not describe sentencing or any appeal. The reporter’s interpretation of Brand closing his eyes is speculative, and the identity of the lookalike is never explained in the source.
items.op: A defendant’s demeanour should never influence a jury, and this account shows why the public must be able to watch trials directly. Open courts let evidence be tested in view of everyone. The public gallery and press benches are not entertainment; they are the safeguard that keeps justice honest.

items.t: Ronaldo’s international retirement draws verdict that his long farewell tarnished a great career
items.s: Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international football, and Guardian columnist Jonathan Wilson argues that he stayed too long, leaving a legacy shaped by a drawn-out exit. Tributes from Portugal, his clubs and football’s governing body have followed.
p: Wilson opens with the difficulty elite athletes face in choosing when to stop. He argues that the self-belief that carries top sportspeople to the summit can make it hard for them to accept that the time has come. Ronaldo’s retirement, he writes, is a loss for football, and also a reminder of mortality, but he regrets the timing.

The column traces the problem back to the 2022 World Cup. According to Wilson, Fernando Santos left Ronaldo out of the last-16 tie against Switzerland, and Portugal looked fluent for the first time in years, with Gonçalo Ramos scoring a hat-trick. Even so, many fans in the stadium kept chanting for Ronaldo, and he later scored an offside goal and celebrated with his “Siuuuu” routine.

Wilson also says Ronaldo’s status made him a political question. He reports that a cabinet minister argued the striker could not be dropped because of the revenue he generated and his value to Portugal’s image.

Wilson’s account of the most recent years is harsher. He describes Ronaldo weeping after missing a penalty against Slovenia at Euro 2024. At the most recent World Cup, Wilson says, Ronaldo was often out of position and lacked the pace of his peak, and he cites a chance against Spain that was lost when Ronaldo had to turn back.

Wilson says the national team needed a change. He reports that Jorge Jesus, a 72-year-old coach appointed after the World Cup, did not bring Ronaldo off the bench in the second half of a tight win over Norway. Ronaldo said he had been promised minutes, and he left the squad. The column reports a fine of €255 (£212) and a 30-day ban, imposed in a period when Portugal had no games.

Tributes followed the announcement. The Portuguese Football Federation praised his dedication and legacy, and Al-Nassr called him an icon. Manchester United, Bruno Fernandes, Diogo Dalot, Pepe and Fifa president Gianni Infantino also paid tribute, with Infantino describing Ronaldo’s international career as part of football’s history.

Wilson concludes that Ronaldo will be remembered as one of the all-time greats and as a rival to Eusébio as Portugal’s finest player. Yet, in his view, the long goodbye has damaged his reputation. He adds that Ronaldo will return to the Saudi Pro League, where he is chasing a 1,000th career goal.
items.cav: This is an opinion column, and the account of the fine, the ban and the alleged promise of minutes comes from the writer and has not been independently confirmed here. Wilson also says Ronaldo’s retirement might be a power play to force Jesus out, but he does not establish that.
items.op: Selection decisions in national teams should rest on clear, open reasoning, not on a player’s fame or commercial value. When a star’s place is protected by reputation, the squad and the public both lose. Accountability should apply to legends too.

items.t: Fresh bomb hoaxes disrupt European flights again in a week of threats
items.s: Flights across Europe were hit by bomb threats on Thursday, the second such round this week. Some planes were diverted and others were escorted by fighter jets, and searches reportedly found no explosives.
p: According to the BBC, at least 15 flights were affected on Thursday. Routes bound for Italy, Poland, Bulgaria, Austria and the Czech Republic were among those involved, and the threats came in the same week as an earlier wave.

One closely watched case involved an Aer Lingus service that left Dublin for Rome. It was redirected to an air base at Evreux in northern France on Thursday morning, and the airline said it landed safely. Separately, a Finnair flight from Helsinki was accompanied into Rome by Italian military jets and touched down on schedule.

Earlier in the week, eight European flights, two of them from Britain, were targeted by suspected threats. Searches of those aircraft did not uncover explosives. Czech police reported the same outcome for four flights that landed in Prague, while Bulgarian media said three Ryanair flights were escorted by air force jets before landing in Sofia and Plovdiv.
EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas said it was not yet clear whether the incidents were connected. UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander described them as deliberate hoaxes.

Airport authorities in Rome said the threat against two inbound flights arrived by email. The sender signed it on behalf of a group or individual calling itself “Fighters of the Male State”, which said it was targeting a “feminist regime”. Italian media first reported these details, and Aeroporti di Roma, which runs both of the city’s airports, confirmed them to the BBC.

Aviation specialists quoted by the BBC offered differing readings. Philip Baum of the University of Coventry said he was surprised by the incidents and warned that a run of hoaxes could breed complacency, so that a genuine threat gets overlooked. Marco Chan of Kingston University said the threats were probably hoaxes, but that treating them as real was the right response. He noted that some experts linked them to a wider pattern of low-cost disruption, and cautioned that three days is too short a period to tell coordinated action from copycats.
Separately, the BBC reported that on Monday a Wizz Air flight from London Luton to Sofia was escorted to Budapest by a Hungarian fighter jet after a mid-air threat.
items.cav: The 15-flight figure appears only in the BBC’s summary and is not itemised. The sources do not identify the group behind the email threats or establish any link to the other incidents. Several details, including the Rome reports of anonymous tips, are second-hand.
items.op: Threats against passengers demand more than reassurance. The public has a right to know what investigators have established about who is sending these messages and whether the incidents are connected. Calling them hoaxes may prove accurate, but the label settles nothing until authorities show their working.

items.t: Bomb threats divert flights across Europe as EU says too early to link incidents
items.s: Several commercial flights were diverted or forced to land across Europe on Thursday after bomb threats, days after a similar wave of hoaxes. Authorities reported no devices were found, and the EU has not established whether the incidents are connected.
p: The disruption followed a run of threats on Tuesday that led to emergency searches and a brief closure of an airport outside Warsaw. Live reporting by The Guardian counted 18 affected flights on Thursday, while Al Jazeera cited about 12. The tallies differ between outlets and may change as more reports arrive.

French authorities said an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was steered to Evreux after a suspected threat and accompanied by military aircraft. The office of Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said a bomb squad was on site and that 151 passengers and six crew had been brought to safety. Elsewhere, a Ryanair service from London Stansted to Sofia was diverted to Plovdiv in Bulgaria, and a WizzAir flight from Milan Malpensa to Warsaw was rerouted to Vienna, where the airline said it followed its standard safety procedures.

A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted by a fighter jet and inspected by bomb disposal experts, an airport spokesman told AFP. Italy’s Ansa news agency, citing police sources, said the warning about the Helsinki and Dublin flights arrived in an anonymous email, written in Italian, that was sent to the company that runs Rome’s airports and affiliated firms.

Spanish authorities said three flights were affected by hoax threats at Madrid’s airport, and that security forces had ruled out any risk. In Bulgaria, three aircraft asked for emergency landings after threats, and inspections found no problems. Czech police said aircraft bound for Prague were searched, with negative results, and that the case has passed to the National Centre against Terrorism, Extremism and Cybercrime. In Brussels, a LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw landed safely after a security warning, and its crew found nothing suspicious on board.

EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas said it was “too early to draw conclusions” on whether the incidents were linked, while condemning threats against civilians. Aviation analysts quoted by The Guardian noted that fake threats occur every day, yet the number judged credible suggests coordinated action. One analyst described the campaign as loosely organised, with no clear regional focus. Al Jazeera’s correspondent said nobody had yet been identified as responsible.

Al Jazeera also placed the episode in a wider frame, recalling that the German government has blamed Russia for a failed drone attack on Leipzig airport in August. The outlet found no evidence tying the current threats to that attack or to other recent incidents, though it said European governments are likely to examine such links.
items.cav: The sources disagree on the number of affected flights: about 12 in Al Jazeera, 15 in a Guardian headline, and 18 in its live tally. Many details, including the Madrid flights and the Romanian clearance of a WizzAir flight, rely on official statements or second-hand reports, and no source has identified who sent the threats.
items.op: Hoax threats that force planes to land and frighten passengers are not harmless pranks, and governments owe the public clear information. Authorities should publish what they know about the emails and calls, and whether they share a source. Openness now will do more to restore confidence in air travel than reassurance alone.

items.t: Melania Trump to host Russian and Ukrainian delegations at White House after Oleshky truce
items.s: US First Lady Melania Trump will host Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday, a day after Ukraine honoured her with the Order of Princess Olha. Washington credits her with brokering a ceasefire, but neither Moscow nor Kyiv has explained how far her role went.
p: Officials from Moscow and Kyiv are set to be received by the first lady in Washington on Thursday. The gathering precedes negotiations in Abu Dhabi that are intended to bring the Ukraine war to an end. Hopes for a settlement have been revived, even as the invasion approaches its fifth year and closer ties between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have prompted worries that the United States might abandon Kyiv.

On Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky signed a decree conferring the Order of Princess Olha, First Class, on Melania Trump. The document praised her contribution to humanitarian aid for Ukraine and her work on human rights and charity, citing in particular her efforts on behalf of Ukrainian children affected by the conflict.

The honour follows a limited truce in the Kherson region that enabled several hundred people to leave Oleshky, a city under Russian occupation where supplies of food and medicine had run short for weeks. According to Euronews, the first lady announced the truce last month, and both armies observed it, which allowed roads to be cleared of mines. BBC reporting indicates that the truce has since expired.

The White House says she started contact between the two countries on her own initiative and secured the pause in fighting, describing it as a first of its kind for an American first lady. Russian and Ukrainian officials both credited her with arranging the truce, yet neither has spelled out what her involvement actually consisted of.

Kyiv is expected to send ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and parliamentarian Davyd Arakhamia, who has sat on Ukraine’s negotiating team before. The Kremlin, through spokesman Dmitry Peskov, has named ombudsman Yana Lantratova and Kirill Dmitriev, a businessman with close ties to the Kremlin, as Moscow’s representatives. Euronews reported that the Russian attendance depended on logistics being settled. Lubinets and Lantratova had entered Oleshky together the previous week.

No agenda for the White House meeting has been made public. The first lady is due to address the Oleshky truce that day, according to the White House website. Zelensky also reported lengthy talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in preparation for the Abu Dhabi round, which would be the first gathering of all three parties since February.

The UN has earlier this year described the forced transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia as a crime against humanity and a war crime. Kyiv claims nearly 20,000 children have been unlawfully moved to Russia and Belarus since 2022. In 2025 the first lady said she had set up a channel of dialogue with Putin to help reunite children with their families, but otherwise she has kept a low profile on foreign policy.
items.cav: The sources do not say what the White House meeting will involve, and the first lady’s role in the truce rests on claims from her office and both governments, not independent confirmation. BBC and Euronews also disagree on whether the truce still holds, and give different times for her remarks (16:00 GMT versus 1700 GMT).
items.op: Honours and praise cannot stand in for accountability. When an official without a public mandate is credited with brokering a ceasefire, the public deserves to know what she did, who took part, and what was agreed. Talks on a war that has displaced children should be open to scrutiny, not shaped by vague claims of influence.

items.t: Trump accepts midterm results as Democrats win broadly and Republicans face a reckoning
items.s: Donald Trump has accepted the results of the US midterm elections, which the Guardian describes as a sweeping win for Democrats. Analysis of the vote points to the Iran war as a major factor in the Republican losses.
p: According to the Guardian’s newsletter coverage, Trump has accepted the midterm results, and the electoral system held up against attempts at election interference. His administration had earlier worked to cast doubt on the outcome, but the worst fears did not materialise, the newsletter says.

An unnamed Trump adviser told CNN that the result was too large to manipulate, after Democrats took power across the country. Trump appeared in public the day after the vote, mainly to discuss plans for a new White House ballroom.

The Guardian’s own analysis found that dozens of Republican candidates whom Trump had directly endorsed lost their races, raising questions about the reach of his backing. Senator Susan Collins, who had held her seat in Maine for nearly three decades, was defeated.

Pete Hegseth, the defence secretary, may be made the scapegoat for the party’s losses, with the war in Iran cited as a key reason for the weak showing. JD Vance has reportedly distanced himself from the decision to strike Iran alongside Israel, and a Democratic-controlled Congress is expected to try to limit future US foreign military action.

Democrats also gained hundreds of seats in state legislatures. Voters approved nearly every datacentre moratorium on the ballot, while Colorado rejected a conservative measure that would have required police to cooperate with immigration officers. Nevada, Virginia, Missouri and Idaho passed or strengthened protections for reproductive freedom.
Fox News reported a ratings slump after the vote, and an analysis by Nick Robins-Early described nearly half a billion dollars in midterm spending by Elon Musk as a flop.
items.cav: The Guardian’s figures on endorsed candidates come from its own analysis, and the claim that Hegseth may take the blame is speculation. The adviser’s remark is second-hand, relayed through CNN, and the sources do not say who the adviser is.
items.op: Accepting a result is the minimum a democracy requires, and it deserves credit. The harder test is whether Congress now uses its powers to scrutinise the war in Iran openly, rather than letting the voters’ verdict fade into rhetoric.

items.t: Cristiano Ronaldo announces retirement from international football after row with Portugal coach
items.s: Cristiano Ronaldo has said he will no longer play for Portugal, closing a national-team career that holds the men’s records for appearances and goals. The announcement comes weeks after a dispute with coach Jorge Jesus over playing time.
p: Ronaldo revealed the decision on Thursday in a lengthy video posted to his Instagram account. The 41-year-old said he was giving back the No. 7 shirt after 23 years of wearing it for his country.

Across his national career, Ronaldo made 234 appearances for Portugal and scored 146 goals, figures that make him the record holder for both categories among men. He captained the team to Euro 2016, its first major title, and later helped it win the Nations League in 2019 and 2025.

In the message, he said the choice had been difficult and that it had been shaped by emotion as well as reason. He thanked his family, the Portuguese public, and the teammates, coaches and staff he had worked with over the years.

The Portuguese Football Association (FPF) praised him in a statement, describing him as a figure who had raised the country’s profile and motivated young players. The federation said it plans to hold a tribute so supporters can honour him again.

The rift began in September. Ronaldo’s last game for Portugal was a 1-0 win over Wales in the Nations League on September 24. Jesus then dropped him to the bench for the next fixture and indicated he would not start the one after that, and Ronaldo left the training camp.

The accounts differ on what came next. DW reported that the FPF suspended and fined Ronaldo, and that he had been expected back for the November break. Euronews said Jesus later told reporters Ronaldo would be welcome to return, with the decision left to the player. France 24 wrote that the coach had refused to use him in a match.

Like Lionel Messi, who recently played a farewell match for Argentina, Ronaldo will continue at club level. He is expected to end his club career with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia at the close of this season.
items.cav: The sources disagree on the dispute: some say Jesus left Ronaldo on the bench, while France 24 says the coach refused to use him. The suspension and fine come only from DW, and the tribute’s date and format have not been announced.
items.op: A player may choose when his national career ends, but a row that ends in a walkout deserves a clear public account, not just a farewell video. Fans and federations are owed transparency about the suspension and the terms of any return. The FPF should set out those facts before any tribute turns the final chapter into a celebration.

items.t: Cristiano Ronaldo quits Portugal duty in farewell video after months of friction with coach
items.s: Cristiano Ronaldo has told Portuguese fans he is ending his international career. The announcement follows a fine, a suspension and a public dispute with coach Jorge Jesus.
p: Cristiano Ronaldo has said he is stepping away from the national team, according to an Instagram video in which he addressed Portuguese supporters directly. The 41-year-old forward holds the world records for goals (146) and caps (234) for his country, which he has collected since his debut in 2003.

The exit comes after a turbulent few months. In September, Ronaldo walked out of the squad when he learned he would not start a Nations League game against Denmark. The Portuguese Football Federation (PFF) handed him a £215 fine and a 30-day ban, though the BBC reports that none of Portugal's matches fell within that window.

Before the video, Ronaldo had put out a long statement insisting he had no plans to retire. In it he accused Jesus of breaking his word on two occasions. The coach responded that he would welcome Ronaldo back. In the farewell clip, Ronaldo did not refer to the row, though he admitted he had made errors.

His last tournament ended badly. He featured in every game of his sixth World Cup this summer, a campaign that finished when Portugal were knocked out in the last 16 by Spain, who went on to win the title. Media commentators had questioned whether he could still perform at the highest level. Reports also say he was furious after being told to warm up in the second half against Norway without being sent on, the first time since 2008 he had been left out of a competitive Portugal match as a substitute.

Ronaldo has taken part in six European Championships. Portugal were beaten finalists in 2004 and lifted the trophy in 2016, but failed to get past the World Cup semi-finals during his time with the side. He has worn the captain's armband since 2008 and was part of the winning teams at the Nations League in 2019 and 2025.

The PFF has said it will not allow his departure to pass without a proper tribute and that it wants to help plan and host one. Portugal are due to announce their squad on Friday for this month's Nations League fixtures, which are at home to Denmark and away to Wales.
Ronaldo's great rival, Lionel Messi, also ended his international career this year, doing so in October before a crowd of 85,000 in Buenos Aires.
items.cav: The retirement is known from Ronaldo's own video, and the sources do not say whether the PFF has confirmed the details of any tribute. The dispute with Jesus rests on Ronaldo's statement and on reports of his anger, and the coach's side is only summarised, not quoted in full. His earlier insistence that he would not retire sits uneasily with this announcement.
items.op: A farewell should not bury the questions a career leaves behind. Ronaldo's record deserves honour, but the fine, the suspension and the public clash with his coach are part of how his exit happened. Football's authorities owe fans a clear account of those events, not just a ceremony.

items.t: Cristiano Ronaldo announces end of Portugal career with 234 caps and 146 goals
items.s: Cristiano Ronaldo has said he will no longer play for Portugal, closing an international career that included six World Cups, a European title and the men’s all-time scoring record. He made the announcement in a lengthy video posted on social media.
p: The 41-year-old framed the decision as a handover to the next generation, describing his years in the national side as a responsibility he carried into stadiums around the world. He said the choice was difficult, weighing emotion as well as reason, and traced his career back to his debut in August 2003.

His last appearance for Portugal, according to the report, came on 24 September, a 1-0 victory over Wales in the Nations League. Coach Jorge Jesus then left him out of the squad for the next game and indicated he would not be in the starting line-up for the one after that.

Ronaldo subsequently withdrew from the training camp. The report says the break followed a dispute with Jesus, though Jesus later stated that Ronaldo would be welcome back and that returning was his own decision.

The Portuguese Football Federation said it was grateful for his service and admired his contribution. It credited him with raising the country’s profile and inspiring young players, and it said it plans a tribute event that would let supporters honour him once more.

Across his national career, Ronaldo made 234 appearances and scored a record 146 goals, the report notes. The comparison with Lionel Messi was drawn here: Messi ended his international career with Argentina after a farewell match last month.

Ronaldo will carry on at club level and is expected to conclude his club career at the end of the current season with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia. He is working towards 1,000 career goals and currently has 985.
items.cav: The sources describe the falling-out with Jesus only second-hand and do not give either side’s full account of the dispute. The exact reasons for the break, and whether Ronaldo would ever return, are not clear from the reporting.
items.op: A player’s farewell should be decided openly, not shaped by a quarrel in a training camp. Ronaldo has earned a dignified exit, and the federation’s promised tribute should honour his record without hiding how the final months unfolded. Clear accounts from all sides matter.

items.t: Tech billionaires face a harder road as Democrats take Congress in the midterms
items.s: Democrats’ midterm gains were helped by voter anger over tech, the rich and the super rich, according to a Guardian commentary, and the tech elite that backed Donald Trump now faces investigations and pressure.
p: The Guardian commentary argues that the photo of Silicon Valley’s richest figures at Donald Trump’s inauguration, with Elon Musk, Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg seated side by side, now looks less like a show of alliance and more like a list of targets for a Congress led by Democrats.

Democrats took decisive control of the US Congress on Tuesday, flipping seats that had previously seemed safe for Republicans. They also won governors’ mansions across the country, including in Texas, a state the article describes as one of the reddest.

The piece says voters concerned about corruption punished politicians seen as serving the interests of wealthy tech figures. Texas Democratic representative Greg Casar wrote that voters rejected Republicans in part because they were “bought and paid for” by billionaires from the tech sector, and urged his party to hold them accountable.

Democrats have promised congressional investigations into tech companies and moratoriums on large datacenters. Gina Hinojosa of Texas, Amy Acton of Ohio and Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia have all pledged pauses, and letters asking Nvidia and Amazon to preserve records have reportedly already been sent.

Musk, who the article says gave $450m to Republican candidates, most of it to Ken Paxton in Texas, had a difficult night. Paxton lost by a wide margin, and Musk later deleted a Tuesday post urging people to vote Republican. The article also notes that Democrats may look at a multibillion dollar merger of SpaceX with another Musk-led company, which holds a $200m contract with the US military.

The commentary says Zuckerberg could face the kind of inquiry he went through at the end of the 2010s, pointing to his shift to the right under Trump, including his visit to Mar-a-Lago and the end of Meta’s diversity, equity and inclusion program. It describes Sam Altman, the head of one of the leading firms in the sector, as appearing to distance himself from Trump’s approach to regulation of the industry.

The article concludes that these billionaires are unlikely to repair their public image quickly, because they have said little about affordability and corruption, the issues voters care about most. Its author asks what a billionaire can offer a public angry about prices.
items.cav: This is a commentary piece, so its predictions about investigations, Zuckerberg and Altman are speculative rather than reported. The $450m figure and the $200m contract value are as stated in the article and are not independently confirmed here.
items.op: Public scrutiny of concentrated wealth and private influence over government is a legitimate demand. It should be pursued through open hearings, published records and the same legal standards that apply to everyone else. Investigations driven by political theatre would weaken the transparency voters are asking for.

items.t: Joshua Wong sentenced to further 10 years under Hong Kong national security law
items.s: Former pro-democracy figure Joshua Wong has been jailed for 10 more years for foreign collusion, his second conviction under the city’s national security law. Critics say the case shows the law is being used to silence dissent.
p: Hong Kong’s High Court on Thursday sentenced Joshua Wong, now 30, to 10 years in prison after he pleaded guilty in September to colluding with foreign forces. According to the BBC, prosecutors said Wong conspired with exiled activist Nathan Law and others to lobby foreign governments for sanctions and blockades against Beijing. The activity took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard.

Presiding judge William Tam said he had considered a 13-year starting point but reduced it to 10 because of Wong’s guilty plea and mitigation, according to Al Jazeera. Tam also said Wong’s role was to supply “underground support” and draw foreign attention to the cause. The new term will run concurrently with the remainder of Wong’s existing sentence, the BBC reported.

Wong is already serving four years and eight months, imposed in November 2024 for conspiracy to commit subversion over an unofficial primary election. He had been due for release in January 2027. DW reported that the offence of foreign collusion can carry life imprisonment if judged to be of a serious nature, and that Wong has said he never advocated independence for Hong Kong or regime change in China.

Hong Kong’s chief executive, John Lee, said Wong and Law were among the main culprits responsible for undermining the city’s prosperity and stability. Beijing’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, urged “relevant parties” to respect China’s sovereignty and the city’s legal system, and to stop making irresponsible remarks about the case.

The United States consulate in Hong Kong “strongly condemns” the sentence and called for Wong’s immediate release, saying he had been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020. Taiwan’s top China policy body also criticised what it called endless political persecution of Hong Kong democracy activists. Amnesty International said the sentence was another reminder that the law has become a tool to punish dissent, a view echoed by Human Rights Watch’s Asia director, Elaine Pearson.

Wong rose to prominence as a teenager, co-founding the Scholarism student group in 2011 and helping to lead the 2014 Umbrella Movement. He later co-founded the Demosisto party with Law, which disbanded in 2020 as the national security law took effect. Authorities argue the law is needed to maintain stability and say it has not weakened the city’s autonomy, while critics say it has silenced opposition.

Wong’s friend Frances Hui, who is now based in the United States, told the BBC she was heartbroken and outraged by the verdict, describing it as part of a broader political crackdown. Former media tycoon Jimmy Lai received a 20-year sentence under the same law, the BBC noted, making his the harshest term handed down so far.
items.cav: Sources differ on the exact release date, describing it as January, early next year or January 2027. Wong’s claim that he never sought independence or regime change comes from him and DW reports it without independent confirmation. The sources do not give the full text of the court’s reasoning.
items.op: A sentence for lobbying foreign governments is a sentence for speech, and that should trouble anyone who values open debate. Hong Kong’s courts must show that the law targets genuine threats, not political opposition. Ten more years for a man already behind bars will not reassure a city that has been told its freedoms are secure.

items.t: Democrats win control of Congress in midterms, dealing a blow to Trump and his party
items.s: Republicans lost control of both the Senate and the House in the US midterm elections, with Democrats flipping seats in traditionally Republican states. Some races and House seats were still undecided when reports were published.
p: According to The Guardian, the United States woke up to a changed political landscape after Donald Trump’s Republican Party lost control of the Senate and the House. With counting still under way in a few Senate races and 68 House seats not yet called, Democrats were assured of a congressional majority that was larger than most pundits had predicted.

The Guardian reported that Democrats had flipped at least seven Senate seats, including in Texas and Kansas, and more than two dozen House districts. Among the results it highlighted, James Talarico became the first Democrat Texas has sent to the Senate since 1988, and Gina Hinojosa defeated Governor Greg Abbott to become the first Democratic governor of Texas in 36 years.

Other contests also went against the Republicans, according to the same report. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, a doctor, won the Senate race against Mike Rogers and is described as the country’s first Muslim senator. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton was reported to be the first Democrat to win a Senate seat there in almost a century. In South Carolina, Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham, and in Maine, Susan Collins conceded to Troy Jackson. The Senate race in Mississippi was described as too close to call.

Vice-President JD Vance blamed the defeat on the war with Iran, writing on X that “the reason we lost is the war.” Asked whether he agreed, Trump told reporters he thought the assessment was largely true because it had pushed up petrol prices, though he said he would fight the war again. Voters were also reported to be angry about the cost of living and inflation, which the Guardian linked to Trump’s tariffs.

House Speaker Mike Johnson indicated he will not seek to remain leader of the Republican group when Democrats take over in January. Trump spoke from the site of his White House ballroom project, focusing on construction rather than the election result, and the White House posted that “TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT.” Trump later wrote on social media that he was not on the ballot and that if he had been, his party would have won in a landslide.

The Guardian also reported, citing unnamed accounts, that Trump watched the results at the White House and was fuming. These details come second-hand from the newspaper’s reporting and were not confirmed in the material available.
items.cav: The Al Jazeera item available was only a short summary and gave no further detail. Several results were still being counted at the time of reporting, and Mississippi was too close to call. The claims about Trump’s private reaction are second-hand.
items.op: Voters have delivered a clear verdict, and a healthy democracy depends on the losing side accepting it. Trump’s claim that he was not on the ballot does not change the result. The real test now is whether the incoming Congress uses its oversight powers openly and holds the administration to account.

items.t: After midterm losses, Trump may look abroad, BBC analysis warns of Iran and Ukraine risks
items.s: The BBC's international editor argues that Donald Trump's heavy midterm defeat limits his power at home but may push him toward bolder moves abroad, particularly on Iran and Ukraine. The piece is analysis and speculation about his next steps, not a report of decisions already taken.
p: According to the BBC’s international editor, Trump’s defeat in the midterm elections, in which he lost both houses of the US Congress, restricts his ability to dictate and manoeuvre at home. As commander-in-chief he still holds broad powers over America’s armed forces, and the analysis suggests he may be tempted to use them to offset the electoral setback.

The BBC describes the deployment of US forces and Trump’s often belligerent statements as having raised talk of a return to war with Iran in the weeks before the vote. It reports that the US carried out a limited bombing raid on an Iranian island in the Gulf on the eve of the elections.

Senator Chris Murphy, a Democrat, attended a classified briefing on possible military options against Iran before he was hospitalised with a stroke. The BBC says he condemned the plans as “insane”, without giving details, and warned of a “devastating escalation”.

The analysis says there has been speculation that the United States could bomb civilian infrastructure. It notes that such action would likely be a war crime and could prompt Iranian strikes on targets in Gulf states, with the United Arab Emirates named as a possible target.

Tehran, the BBC says, is watching the political fallout in Washington closely, and has not hidden its satisfaction that the effects of its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have become a domestic issue in the US. The Speaker of Iran’s parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, wrote on social media that Americans had said no to war.

The piece also reports, citing reports in Israel and the US, that Benjamin Netanyahu, acting prime minister after last week’s election, is pushing Trump to return to war with Iran. Netanyahu does not currently have the seats to form a new government with his outgoing coalition, the analysis adds, but a renewed war could change his options.

On Ukraine, the BBC says Trump has shown little concern for civilian casualties from Russian ballistic missiles and has not answered Kyiv’s requests for more US-made interceptors in the way Ukraine wants. The Kremlin said it hoped the election would not affect Trump’s “peace-making efforts”, and the analysis suggests Trump may increase pressure on President Volodymyr Zelensky to accept territorial concessions.
items.cav: This is analysis from the BBC’s international editor, and most of the forward-looking claims are predictions rather than reported decisions. The reports about Netanyahu’s lobbying and the account of Senator Murphy’s briefing are second-hand, and the sources do not give details of the planned military options.
items.op: Power that escapes scrutiny is dangerous, and a leader who loses an election should not be free to rebuild his standing with force. Washington’s lawmakers and the public must demand clear justification for any strike on Iran or pressure on Ukraine, because civilians in the Gulf and Ukraine would bear the cost.

items.t: Democrats win control of both US congressional chambers in midterms, with celebrities cheering
items.s: Democrats regained control of both the House and the Senate in the US midterm elections, according to multiple outlets. Celebrities and party figures reacted with celebration, while the Democratic National Committee chair argued the result gives his party a mandate.
p: Democrats have been celebrating across the United States after a series of victories that, according to Al Jazeera, gave them control of both chambers of Congress. The Guardian reported that the party regained control of both the House and the Senate.

The Guardian described the night as a string of major victories, which it said reflected voters’ disapproval of Donald Trump and his economy. The outlet reported that the result was historic, though the sources it cites for that framing are largely commentary from supporters.

Among the reactions Guardian reported were posts from actors and musicians. Viola Davis celebrated Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became the first Black female governor in US history, according to the article. Danny Trejo praised Xavier Becerra, who the actor said became California’s first Latino governor.

Some reactions were more pointed. John Cusack called for Trump’s impeachment and removal and praised Abdul El-Sayed as a “smart progressive” candidate. Author Stephen King wrote “Buyers’ remorse” after the wins, while James Woods criticised Republicans who, he wrote, “let it happen”.

NPR’s coverage, based on its summary, reports that Democrats flipped Senate seats in Republican strongholds. In an interview, DNC chair Ken Martin said he believes voters gave his party a mandate and set out what comes next. The available summary does not give the details of his argument.

Much of the celebrity commentary is opinion rather than reporting, and the sources do not give final seat counts, margins or turnout figures. The claims about which candidates won specific races come from the outlets and the posters themselves.
items.cav: The NPR material is limited to a summary, so Ken Martin’s full argument is not available here. The celebrity reactions are personal opinion, and the sources do not provide final seat totals or margins.
items.op: Winning a majority is not the same as a mandate for everything a party wants. Voters chose candidates, not a blanket endorsement, so the winners should be judged by transparent records and the rule of law. Celebration is cheap; accountability in office is what will show whether this victory meant anything.

items.t: Hackers Tampered With Freezers Storing Blood in France, as Attribution Remains Unclear
items.s: French authorities say hackers affected fridges used to store donated blood, and the French Blood Establishment reports no health impact so far. Security researchers are still working out who was responsible.
p: The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were affected by hackers, with temperatures set to rise. According to the agency, staff intervened to protect the supplies. “No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported,” the EFS said.

Until now, supermarkets were the only sites publicly known to have been hit by the attacks, which the BBC reports have affected several European countries. The blood storage incident widens the set of targets.

Online rumours have pointed to Russian hacktivist groups. Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they had hacked Danfoss, a equipment maker, which led some to suspect them of the freezer attacks. Analysts now question whether that claim links them to the supermarket attacks at all. Experts say Iranian hacktivists, state-backed hackers or even teenagers playing pranks could also be responsible.

Several cyber-security firms have set up honeypots, which are decoy systems designed to look like vulnerable freezer software and to record how attackers behave. Ryan Dewhurst of Previdian said the fact that all the devices were hit at the same time suggests planning and coordination. He also said the attackers would have needed to compile a list of public IP addresses and choose their methods carefully.

Lupovis, a Strathclyde-based firm, said its honeypots began to see activity about ten days before the second wave. Its founder, Dr Xavier Bellekens, said the scanning and probing were aimed only at targets in Europe, with none of the decoys in places such as Africa or South America attacked. Sekoia, a French firm, also saw scanning before the second wave, but said it might have been automated and not malicious.

Sekoia’s report said the attacks resembled activity linked to Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, but it also pointed to Iranian-aligned actors. It noted that about 40 Israeli supermarkets using Danfoss controllers were compromised in 2022. Separately, freezers at at least six US military bases were reportedly pushed into defrost mode in late August, though the controller models have not been confirmed and investigations are continuing. A Sekoia spokesperson said, “To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups.”
items.cav: The sources do not establish who carried out the attacks, and the hacktivist claims about Danfoss are unverified. The US base incident and the Israeli supermarket case are reported second-hand, and the controller models involved in the US incident are unconfirmed.
items.op: Critical infrastructure that keeps donated blood cold should not depend on poorly protected software. Governments and manufacturers owe the public a clear account of what failed, who was affected and how it will be fixed. Attribution matters, but so does transparency about the basic security failures.

items.t: Stocks and bonds rally as Democrats win control of Congress; technology and defence shares move sharply
items.s: Markets in the US and Europe rose after Democrats secured control of Congress in the midterm elections, according to a Guardian live blog. Investors are hoping the new majority will limit sudden policy shifts and curb government spending.
p: European shares climbed on the news. The FTSE 100 in London rose about 2%, to 10,845, while the Dax in Frankfurt gained a similar amount. Wall Street was expected to open higher, and the Dow Jones, S&P 500 and Nasdaq were all reported up in the blog’s updates.

Government bonds also rallied, pushing yields lower in the US, UK, Italy and Germany. The blog reported that the 10-year US Treasury yield fell to about 4.90%, and the German yield, the eurozone benchmark, slipped to 3.29%, which it said indicated easing borrowing costs for governments.

Sector moves were sharp. Amazon and Alphabet jumped, while Tesla and SpaceX fell. Shares in companies such as CoreWeave and several datacentre operators slid on the prospect of tighter regulation of the sector. The blog noted that Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates, including in Texas.

Defence stocks fell on both sides of the Atlantic. Trump’s $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget request is expected to face closer scrutiny in Congress, and the blog cited losses at Northrop Grumman, RTX and Lockheed Martin, as well as a drop of about 6% at BAE Systems earlier in the session.

Democrats also won the Texas and Georgia governor races, both in states where local opposition to large data centres has been growing. The new Texas governor, Gina Hinojosa, has repeatedly called for a moratorium on new datacentres, according to the blog.
Oil was volatile. Brent crude fell towards $100 a barrel as traders awaited Washington’s next move against Iran. The blog did not say what that move might be.

The blog’s figures shift between updates, and some numbers, including the size of the dollar’s fall and the moves in individual stocks, are not consistent across its entries. The reasons for the rally are also the blog’s own reading. Its claim that Trump may face a gridlock-type legislative standoff rests on his comments about vetoes, which it reported without further detail.
items.cav: The figures come from a live blog that updates throughout the day, and they differ between entries, including for the dollar, Brent crude and individual share prices. The reading that gridlock will persist rests on the blog’s interpretation of Trump’s veto remarks and is not confirmed by other sources.
items.op: Markets are rewarding the prospect of a divided check on Trump, but a rally built on expected legislative paralysis is a fragile basis for policy. Investors and voters alike should demand clear, public rules for the data centre and technology sectors now under political pressure, rather than relying on who controls Congress.

items.t: Lame duck or mad dog? Europe weighs what a weakened Trump means after the US midterms
items.s: Democrats’ midterm gains leave President Donald Trump with less domestic authority in his final two years, and European officials fear he may turn to foreign policy to regain the initiative.
p: According to Euronews, Democrats captured both chambers of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections and also won governorships in several states, a result the outlet describes as a severe setback for President Donald Trump. Trump was not a candidate, yet the vote was widely interpreted as a judgment on his administration, which polls show is unpopular.

Euronews reports that European officials are concerned a president with less backing at home could become harder to predict abroad, since foreign policy is an area where he faces fewer checks from Congress. An EU diplomat told the outlet that Trump would be “more a ‘mad dog’ than a ‘lame duck’”, a reference to the label usually given to presidents who face a hostile legislature.

Brando Benifei, an Italian MEP who heads the European Parliament’s delegation for relations with the US, told Euronews that Trump could adopt an even more erratic foreign policy over the next two years. In his view, Washington’s choices on Ukraine and the Middle East would weigh heavily on Europe.

The war in Iran has pushed Europe into an energy crisis and dominates the agenda of EU diplomats and lawmakers. Iran has largely closed the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began on 28 February, with a short reopening in June, and restrictions on shipping keep energy prices high. Romanian MEP Virgil-Daniel Popescu argued that the election result alone will not lower prices; the decisive factor is whether Washington and Tehran move toward de-escalation.

Congress holds the constitutional authority to declare war and can pass measures to halt US military operations. Trump could block such a measure with a veto, and overriding it would take a two-thirds vote in both chambers, a high bar even with Democratic gains. Dimitar Likov of the Wilfried Martens Centre for European Studies said he sees no prospect of de-escalation in the near term.

On Ukraine, Euronews suggests the midterms could bring a notable change in Washington’s stance. Ties between the US and Kyiv were already strained, with Trump facing criticism for permitting Russian diesel imports and for easing sanctions on Moscow. A Democratic-led Congress is expected to push for continued military aid, including air defence systems and ballistic missile interceptors, and for a firmer approach to Moscow. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had not commented publicly on the results, while Russia said it hoped the vote would not disrupt Trump’s push to negotiate a “peace settlement”.

Democrats still face obstacles, including the Senate filibuster and Trump’s veto, and their leverage over US dealings with Moscow would be limited. On troops, Washington announced in May that 5,000 soldiers would leave Germany, and a six-month review of its European force posture began in June, with results expected around year-end. The Pentagon is barred from dropping below 76,000 personnel in Europe in 2026 unless it certifies to Congress that such a cut poses no threat to US or NATO security.
